Ensemble Kalman processes: EKI, ETKI, GNKI, TEKI, EKS and UKI

The filters of chapters 5 to 8 track a state through time. The same algebra also solves a static inverse problem. Given one batch of data, it estimates the parameters of a forward model that may be expensive and may have no derivatives. An ensemble of candidate parameters is iterated, and its own covariances stand in for the Jacobian.

Each process in this chapter is one choice about the same tempered Kalman update, and that choice organises the chapter. EKI moves every member with the same data, so the ensemble collapses onto a point estimate. ETKI and UKI keep the Gaussian moments right, so a linear problem lands exactly on the posterior. GNKI and TEKI bring the prior into the update and head for its mean or mode. EKS adds noise, so the ensemble samples the posterior and never stops. A scheduler then decides how far each iteration goes.

The inverse problem¶

The data are one observation vector y∈RDy\vect{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}y∈RDy​ from

y=h(θ)+ε,ε∼N(0,Σε),θ∼N(μθ,Σθ),\vect{y} = h(\gvect{\theta}) + \gvect{\varepsilon}, \qquad \gvect{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon), \qquad \gvect{\theta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\gvect{\mu}_\theta, \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta),y=h(θ)+ε,ε∼N(0,Σε​),θ∼N(μθ​,Σθ​),
(9.1)

with parameters θ∈RDθ\gvect{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta}θ∈RDθ​, a forward model h:RDθ→RDyh : \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta} \to \mathbb{R}^{D_y}h:RDθ​→RDy​, a noise covariance Σε∈RDy×Dy\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}Σε​∈RDy​×Dy​, and a prior mean μθ∈RDθ\gvect{\mu}_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta}μθ​∈RDθ​ and covariance Σθ∈RDθ×Dθ\gmat{\Sigma}_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta \times D_\theta}Σθ​∈RDθ​×Dθ​. Docstrings call the forward model GGG and the noise Γ\GammaΓ, but G\mat{G}G is the gain here.

Stack the members as rows of Θ∈RNE×Dθ\gmat{\Theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_\theta}Θ∈RNE​×Dθ​, with mean θˉ∈RDθ\bar{\gvect{\theta}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta}θˉ∈RDθ​ and anomalies Θ~∈RNE×Dθ\tilde{\gmat{\Theta}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_\theta}Θ~∈RNE​×Dθ​. Each member maps to h(e)=h(θ(e))\vect{h}^{(e)} = h(\gvect{\theta}^{(e)})h(e)=h(θ(e)), with mean hˉ∈RDy\bar{\vect{h}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}hˉ∈RDy​ and anomalies H~∈RNE×Dy\tilde{\mat{H}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_y}H~∈RNE​×Dy​. With c=NE−1c = N_\mathcal{E} - 1c=NE​−1, the sample covariances are Σ^θ=Θ~⊤Θ~/c\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta = \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^\top \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}} / cΣ^θ​=Θ~⊤Θ~/c, Σ^θy=Θ~⊤H~/c\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{\theta y} = \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^\top \tilde{\mat{H}} / cΣ^θy​=Θ~⊤H~/c and Σ^h=H~⊤H~/c\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_h = \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top \tilde{\mat{H}} / cΣ^h​=H~⊤H~/c.

An iteration iii takes a step Δt(i)>0\Delta t^{(i)} > 0Δt(i)>0 in an artificial time τ(i)=∑k<iΔt(k)\tau^{(i)} = \sum_{k < i} \Delta t^{(k)}τ(i)=∑k<i​Δt(k), which the code calls algo_time. Tempering interpolates the prior at τ=0\tau = 0τ=0 and the posterior at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1:

pτ(θ∣y)∝p(θ)p(y∣θ)τ.p_\tau(\gvect{\theta} \mid \vect{y}) \propto p(\gvect{\theta}) p(\vect{y} \mid \gvect{\theta})^\tau.pτ​(θ∣y)∝p(θ)p(y∣θ)τ.
(9.2)

Raising a Gaussian likelihood to the power Δt\Delta tΔt replaces Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ with Σε/Δt\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon / \Delta tΣε​/Δt.

EKI: one data vector for every member¶

Ensemble Kalman inversion Iglesias et al., 2013 applies a tempered Kalman update to the ensemble. filterax passes the same y\vect{y}y to every member, so the step has no randomness:

G^=Σ^θy(Σ^h+Σε/Δt)−1,θ(e)←θ(e)+G^(y−h(e)).\hat{\mat{G}} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{\theta y} \left(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_h + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon / \Delta t\right)^{-1}, \qquad \gvect{\theta}^{(e)} \leftarrow \gvect{\theta}^{(e)} + \hat{\mat{G}} \left(\vect{y} - \vect{h}^{(e)}\right).G^=Σ^θy​(Σ^h​+Σε​/Δt)−1,θ(e)←θ(e)+G^(y−h(e)).
(9.3)

Here G^∈RDθ×Dy\hat{\mat{G}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta \times D_y}G^∈RDθ​×Dy​, and hhh is only ever evaluated, never differentiated. The step is gaussx.eki_step, which forms the bracket densely when NE≥DyN_\mathcal{E} \ge D_yNE​≥Dy​ and applies Woodbury otherwise, and Σε/Δt\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon / \Delta tΣε​/Δt stays a lazily scaled operator. As Δt→0\Delta t \to 0Δt→0 the increment tends to ΔtΣ^θyΣε−1(y−h(e))\Delta t \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{\theta y} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} (\vect{y} - \vect{h}^{(e)})ΔtΣ^θy​Σε−1​(y−h(e)), the Euler step of a flow in τ\tauτ. For a linear h(θ)=Hθh(\gvect{\theta}) = \mat{H} \gvect{\theta}h(θ)=Hθ we have Σ^θy=Σ^θH⊤\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{\theta y} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \mat{H}^\topΣ^θy​=Σ^θ​H⊤, so the flow is a gradient descent on the data misfit, preconditioned by Σ^θ\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\thetaΣ^θ​.

Every increment is a combination of the anomalies, so the members never leave the affine span of the initial ensemble. That is why EKI runs with NE≤DθN_\mathcal{E} \le D_\thetaNE​≤Dθ​, and also why it can recover nothing outside that span. Program 9.5 checks the property with 5 members and Dθ=10D_\theta = 10Dθ​=10.

EKI does not follow the tempered posterior¶

The common y\vect{y}y has a cost. Subtract the mean of (9.3) from a linear hhh and the anomalies obey Θ~←Θ~(I−G^H)⊤\tilde{\gmat{\Theta}} \leftarrow \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}} (\mat{I} - \hat{\mat{G}} \mat{H})^\topΘ~←Θ~(I−G^H)⊤, which gives

Σ^θ←(I−G^H)Σ^θ(I−G^H)⊤,\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \leftarrow (\mat{I} - \hat{\mat{G}} \mat{H}) \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta (\mat{I} - \hat{\mat{G}} \mat{H})^\top,Σ^θ​←(I−G^H)Σ^θ​(I−G^H)⊤,
(9.4)

where the Kalman update would give (I−G^H)Σ^θ(\mat{I} - \hat{\mat{G}} \mat{H}) \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta(I−G^H)Σ^θ​. The missing term is the one that perturbed observations would add. So one step with Δt=1\Delta t = 1Δt=1 gets the Kalman mean right, and contracts the covariance too far.

Several small steps get both wrong. Write the data precision as Λh=H⊤Σε−1H∈RDθ×Dθ\gmat{\Lambda}_h = \mat{H}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \mat{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta \times D_\theta}Λh​=H⊤Σε−1​H∈RDθ​×Dθ​. Expanding (9.4) to first order in Δt\Delta tΔt gives dΣ^θ/dτ=−2Σ^θΛhΣ^θ\mathrm{d} \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta / \mathrm{d} \tau = -2 \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \gmat{\Lambda}_h \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\thetadΣ^θ​/dτ=−2Σ^θ​Λh​Σ^θ​, and that integrates to

Σ^θ(τ)−1=Σ^θ(0)−1+2τΛh,\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta(\tau)^{-1} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta(0)^{-1} + 2 \tau \gmat{\Lambda}_h,Σ^θ​(τ)−1=Σ^θ​(0)−1+2τΛh​,
(9.5)

with the data counted twice over. The mean follows in closed form when Λh\gmat{\Lambda}_hΛh​ is invertible. Let θLS\gvect{\theta}_\text{LS}θLS​ be the least-squares fit, let Σ^θ(0)=LL⊤\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta(0) = \mat{L} \mat{L}^\topΣ^θ​(0)=LL⊤, and let L⊤ΛhL\mat{L}^\top \gmat{\Lambda}_h \mat{L}L⊤Λh​L have eigenvalues γd\gamma_dγd​ and eigenvectors qd\vect{q}_dqd​. The component zd=qd⊤L−1(θˉ−θLS)z_d = \vect{q}_d^\top \mat{L}^{-1} (\bar{\gvect{\theta}} - \gvect{\theta}_\text{LS})zd​=qd⊤​L−1(θˉ−θLS​) obeys dzd/dτ=−γdzd/(1+2τγd)\mathrm{d} z_d / \mathrm{d} \tau = - \gamma_d z_d / (1 + 2 \tau \gamma_d)dzd​/dτ=−γd​zd​/(1+2τγd​), so at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1

zdEKI=zd(0)1+2γd,zdKalman=zd(0)1+γd.z_d^\text{EKI} = \frac{z_d(0)}{\sqrt{1 + 2 \gamma_d}}, \qquad z_d^\text{Kalman} = \frac{z_d(0)}{1 + \gamma_d}.zdEKI​=1+2γd​​zd​(0)​,zdKalman​=1+γd​zd​(0)​.
(9.6)

So EKI with many small steps does not reach the Kalman answer: its covariance is too small, while its mean stops short because 1+2γd<1+γd\sqrt{1 + 2 \gamma_d} < 1 + \gamma_d1+2γd​​<1+γd​. Program 9.4 measures both. EKI is a regularised point estimator Iglesias, 2016Schillings & Stuart, 2017, and its final spread is not a posterior uncertainty.

ETKI: the moments stay right¶

Ensemble transform Kalman inversion replaces the common y\vect{y}y with the deterministic transform of chapter 6, at the tempered noise. The mean moves as in (9.3), and the anomalies go through a symmetric root:

θˉ←θˉ+G^(y−hˉ),Θ~←c(cI+ΔtH~Σε−1H~⊤)−1/2Θ~.\bar{\gvect{\theta}} \leftarrow \bar{\gvect{\theta}} + \hat{\mat{G}} (\vect{y} - \bar{\vect{h}}), \qquad \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}} \leftarrow \sqrt{c} \left(c \mat{I} + \Delta t \tilde{\mat{H}} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top\right)^{-1/2} \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}.θˉ←θˉ+G^(y−hˉ),Θ~←c​(cI+ΔtH~Σε−1​H~⊤)−1/2Θ~.
(9.7)

By (6.5) the sample covariance after the step is exactly the Kalman one. For a linear hhh and an invertible Σ^θ\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\thetaΣ^θ​ that is a sum in precision form,

Σ^θ−1←Σ^θ−1+ΔtΛh,Σ^θ−1θˉ←Σ^θ−1θˉ+ΔtH⊤Σε−1y,\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{-1} \leftarrow \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{-1} + \Delta t \gmat{\Lambda}_h, \qquad \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{-1} \bar{\gvect{\theta}} \leftarrow \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{-1} \bar{\gvect{\theta}} + \Delta t \mat{H}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \vect{y},Σ^θ−1​←Σ^θ−1​+ΔtΛh​,Σ^θ−1​θˉ←Σ^θ−1​θˉ+ΔtH⊤Σε−1​y,
(9.8)

so any schedule with ∑iΔt(i)=1\sum_i \Delta t^{(i)} = 1∑i​Δt(i)=1 composes to the single Kalman update of the initial mean and sample covariance. This is the tempering of (9.2) done exactly, where (9.5) has a 2 in it.

UKI: sigma points instead of an ensemble¶

Unscented Kalman inversion Huang et al., 2022 keeps a Gaussian belief N(μθ,Σθ)\mathcal{N}(\gvect{\mu}_\theta, \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta)N(μθ​,Σθ​), which starts at the prior and is overwritten at each step. It probes hhh at 2Dθ+12 D_\theta + 12Dθ​+1 deterministic sigma points Wan & van der Merwe, 2000:

χ0=μθ,χ±d=μθ±Dθ+λ[Σθ1/2]d,λ=α2(Dθ+κ)−Dθ,\gvect{\chi}_0 = \gvect{\mu}_\theta, \qquad \gvect{\chi}_{\pm d} = \gvect{\mu}_\theta \pm \sqrt{D_\theta + \lambda} [\gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{1/2}]_d, \qquad \lambda = \alpha^2 (D_\theta + \kappa) - D_\theta,χ0​=μθ​,χ±d​=μθ​±Dθ​+λ​[Σθ1/2​]d​,λ=α2(Dθ​+κ)−Dθ​,
(9.9)

where [⋅]d[\cdot]_d[⋅]d​ is column ddd of the principal root. The mean weights are wm,0=λ/(Dθ+λ)w_{m,0} = \lambda / (D_\theta + \lambda)wm,0​=λ/(Dθ​+λ) and wm,k=1/(2Dθ+2λ)w_{m,k} = 1 / (2 D_\theta + 2 \lambda)wm,k​=1/(2Dθ​+2λ), and the covariance weights differ only at the centre, with wc,0=wm,0+1−α2+βw_{c,0} = w_{m,0} + 1 - \alpha^2 + \betawc,0​=wm,0​+1−α2+β. With hk=h(χk)\vect{h}_k = h(\gvect{\chi}_k)hk​=h(χk​), the weighted moments are hˉ=∑kwm,khk\bar{\vect{h}} = \sum_k w_{m,k} \vect{h}_khˉ=∑k​wm,k​hk​, Σh=∑kwc,k(hk−hˉ)(hk−hˉ)⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_h = \sum_k w_{c,k} (\vect{h}_k - \bar{\vect{h}}) (\vect{h}_k - \bar{\vect{h}})^\topΣh​=∑k​wc,k​(hk​−hˉ)(hk​−hˉ)⊤ and Σθy=∑kwc,k(χk−μθ)(hk−hˉ)⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_{\theta y} = \sum_k w_{c,k} (\gvect{\chi}_k - \gvect{\mu}_\theta) (\vect{h}_k - \bar{\vect{h}})^\topΣθy​=∑k​wc,k​(χk​−μθ​)(hk​−hˉ)⊤, and the update is

Σy=Σh+Σε/Δt,μθ←μθ+ΣθyΣy−1(y−hˉ),Σθ←Σθ−ΣθyΣy−1Σθy⊤.\gmat{\Sigma}_y = \gmat{\Sigma}_h + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon / \Delta t, \qquad \gvect{\mu}_\theta \leftarrow \gvect{\mu}_\theta + \gmat{\Sigma}_{\theta y} \gmat{\Sigma}_y^{-1} (\vect{y} - \bar{\vect{h}}), \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta \leftarrow \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta - \gmat{\Sigma}_{\theta y} \gmat{\Sigma}_y^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_{\theta y}^\top.Σy​=Σh​+Σε​/Δt,μθ​←μθ​+Σθy​Σy−1​(y−hˉ),Σθ​←Σθ​−Σθy​Σy−1​Σθy⊤​.
(9.10)

filterax calls gaussx.sigma_point_kalman_update(..., joseph=False), which is this standard form. The Joseph form that gaussx offers rests on the statistical linearisation H=Σθy⊤Σθ−1\mat{H} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{\theta y}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1}H=Σθy⊤​Σθ−1​, and expanding it with Σθy=GΣy\gmat{\Sigma}_{\theta y} = \mat{G} \gmat{\Sigma}_yΣθy​=GΣy​ gives the same matrix, so the flag only changes the rounding. The sigma-point moments are exact for a linear hhh, so (9.8) holds and the schedule lands on the posterior. The parametric methods init_parametric and update_parametric hold the belief directly, while init and update carry it as sigma points in the particles field, to fit the common protocol.

Two things differ from what the name may suggest. filterax has the default α=1\alpha = 1α=1, where wm,0=0w_{m,0} = 0wm,0​=0, rather than the small α\alphaα common in the unscented literature, for a reason measured in Program 9.12. And it has no prediction step: the artificial dynamics of Huang et al. (2022), which keep their covariance from collapsing, are not implemented, and only tempering remains. So τ=1\tau = 1τ=1 is where the belief is right, and the update keeps contracting past it, as Program 9.6 shows. The Layer 2 UKI stops at τ≥1\tau \ge 1τ≥1, and a Layer 1 loop has to do the same.

GNKI: a Gauss-Newton step to the posterior mean¶

Gauss-Newton Kalman inversion estimates the Jacobian from the ensemble and takes a Gauss-Newton step with a pull towards the prior. It solves against Σ^θ\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\thetaΣ^θ​, so it needs NE>DθN_\mathcal{E} > D_\thetaNE​>Dθ​ and raises an error otherwise:

J^h=Σ^θy⊤(Σ^θ+δI)−1,G=(J^h⊤Σε−1J^h+Σθ−1)−1J^h⊤Σε−1,\hat{\mat{J}}_h = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{\theta y}^\top \left(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta + \delta \mat{I}\right)^{-1}, \qquad \mat{G} = \left(\hat{\mat{J}}_h^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \hat{\mat{J}}_h + \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1}\right)^{-1} \hat{\mat{J}}_h^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1},J^h​=Σ^θy⊤​(Σ^θ​+δI)−1,G=(J^h⊤​Σε−1​J^h​+Σθ−1​)−1J^h⊤​Σε−1​,
(9.11)
θ(e)←θ(e)+Δt[G(y−h(e))+(I−GJ^h)(μθ−θ(e))],\gvect{\theta}^{(e)} \leftarrow \gvect{\theta}^{(e)} + \Delta t \left[\mat{G} (\vect{y} - \vect{h}^{(e)}) + (\mat{I} - \mat{G} \hat{\mat{J}}_h) (\gvect{\mu}_\theta - \gvect{\theta}^{(e)})\right],θ(e)←θ(e)+Δt[G(y−h(e))+(I−GJ^h​)(μθ​−θ(e))],
(9.12)

with J^h∈RDy×Dθ\hat{\mat{J}}_h \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_\theta}J^h​∈RDy​×Dθ​ and an absolute jitter δ\deltaδ, by default 10-6. Take a linear hhh with δ=0\delta = 0δ=0, so that J^h=H\hat{\mat{J}}_h = \mat{H}J^h​=H, and collect the terms in θ(e)\gvect{\theta}^{(e)}θ(e). They cancel, and the bracket is μθ∣y−θ(e)\gvect{\mu}_{\theta \mid y} - \gvect{\theta}^{(e)}μθ∣y​−θ(e), where μθ∣y=μθ+G(y−Hμθ)\gvect{\mu}_{\theta \mid y} = \gvect{\mu}_\theta + \mat{G} (\vect{y} - \mat{H} \gvect{\mu}_\theta)μθ∣y​=μθ​+G(y−Hμθ​) is the exact posterior mean. Every member therefore contracts onto that one point at the same rate:

θ(e)−μθ∣y←(1−Δt)(θ(e)−μθ∣y).\gvect{\theta}^{(e)} - \gvect{\mu}_{\theta \mid y} \leftarrow (1 - \Delta t) \left(\gvect{\theta}^{(e)} - \gvect{\mu}_{\theta \mid y}\right).θ(e)−μθ∣y​←(1−Δt)(θ(e)−μθ∣y​).
(9.13)

GNKI recovers the posterior mean, in one step at Δt=1\Delta t = 1Δt=1, and its spread is not a posterior covariance. The GNKI docstring claims the exact covariance as well, and Program 9.7 shows otherwise.

TEKI: the prior as data¶

Tikhonov EKI Chada et al., 2020 runs (9.3) on a system that observes the parameters too:

h~(θ)=[h(θ)θ],y~=[yμθ],Σ~ε=[Σε00Σθ],\tilde{h}(\gvect{\theta}) = \begin{bmatrix} h(\gvect{\theta}) \\ \gvect{\theta} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \tilde{\vect{y}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vect{y} \\ \gvect{\mu}_\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \tilde{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon & \mat{0} \\ \mat{0} & \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta \end{bmatrix},h~(θ)=[h(θ)θ​],y~​=[yμθ​​],Σ~ε​=[Σε​0​0Σθ​​],
(9.14)

through gaussx.tikhonov_augment, so Σθ\gmat{\Sigma}_\thetaΣθ​ stays an operator inside a block-diagonal one. The least-squares cost of the augmented system is the negative log-posterior,

J(θ)=12∥y−h(θ)∥Σε−12+12∥θ−μθ∥Σθ−12,\mathcal{J}(\gvect{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2} \Vert \vect{y} - h(\gvect{\theta}) \Vert^2_{\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1}} + \frac{1}{2} \Vert \gvect{\theta} - \gvect{\mu}_\theta \Vert^2_{\gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1}},J(θ)=21​∥y−h(θ)∥Σε−1​2​+21​∥θ−μθ​∥Σθ−1​2​,
(9.15)

and for a linear hhh its minimiser θ⋆\gvect{\theta}^\starθ⋆ is a fixed point of the mean, since the normal equations make the projected residual vanish there. So the prior is not forgotten, and the run has no reason to stop at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1.

The convergence is slow, and (9.6) says why. The update is still EKI, and once the spread is small a step of Δt=1\Delta t = 1Δt=1 is a small step of the flow. With γd\gamma_dγd​ now from the augmented data precision, a component of the error falls as (1+2iγd)−1/2(1 + 2 i \gamma_d)^{-1/2}(1+2iγd​)−1/2. The mean reaches the mode at rate i−1/2i^{-1/2}i−1/2, and the spread falls at the same rate. Program 9.8 measures it.

SparseInversion: EKI with a threshold¶

SparseInversion follows the EKI step with a soft threshold, after Schneider et al. (2022):

θd(e)←sign(θd(e))max⁡(∣θd(e)∣−ϱΔt,0),\gvect{\theta}^{(e)}_d \leftarrow \op{sign}(\gvect{\theta}^{(e)}_d) \max\left(\vert \gvect{\theta}^{(e)}_d \vert - \varrho \Delta t, 0\right),θd(e)​←sign(θd(e)​)max(∣θd(e)​∣−ϱΔt,0),
(9.16)

with a penalty ϱ>0\varrho > 0ϱ>0 from the penalty_weight argument. This sets inactive parameters exactly to zero. It also takes ϱΔt\varrho \Delta tϱΔt from every active parameter at every step, while the EKI step shrinks with the spread, so the run length matters, as Program 9.17 measures.

EKS: sampling instead of collapse¶

The ensemble Kalman sampler in its ALDI form Garbuno-Inigo et al., 2020 adds noise and a correction to the continuous flow. That makes it an interacting Langevin diffusion, with the posterior as its stationary law:

dθ(e)=[Σ^θyΣε−1(y−h(e))−Σ^θΣθ−1(θ(e)−μθ)+Dθ+1NE(θ(e)−θˉ)]dτ+2Σ^θdw(e),\mathrm{d} \gvect{\theta}^{(e)} = \left[\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{\theta y} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} (\vect{y} - \vect{h}^{(e)}) - \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1} (\gvect{\theta}^{(e)} - \gvect{\mu}_\theta) + \frac{D_\theta + 1}{N_\mathcal{E}} (\gvect{\theta}^{(e)} - \bar{\gvect{\theta}})\right] \mathrm{d} \tau + \sqrt{2 \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta} \mathrm{d} \vect{w}^{(e)},dθ(e)=[Σ^θy​Σε−1​(y−h(e))−Σ^θ​Σθ−1​(θ(e)−μθ​)+NE​Dθ​+1​(θ(e)−θˉ)]dτ+2Σ^θ​​dw(e),
(9.17)

where w(e)∈RDθ\vect{w}^{(e)} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta}w(e)∈RDθ​ is a Brownian motion. The first term is the EKI drift, the second is the prior, the third corrects for the finite ensemble by pushing members outward, and the noise keeps the spread alive. The third term is the divergence of the ensemble covariance, which noise drawn in ensemble space needs if the posterior is to stay invariant. With no prior arguments the second term is absent and the stationary law is the likelihood alone.

The discrete step has four parts:

  1. The EKI step (9.3), whose tempered gain acts as an implicit Euler step on the data term.

  2. The explicit push +Δt(Dθ+1)/NEΘ~+\Delta t (D_\theta + 1) / N_\mathcal{E} \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}+Δt(Dθ​+1)/NE​Θ~. EKS_Process currently subtracts this term instead, which shrinks the stationary variance on a scalar problem with posterior variance 1 to 0.074 at five members and 0.53 at ten (#173). The EKS numbers in this chapter are measured with the code as it stands, so they carry that error.

  3. The noise, drawn in ensemble space. With N∈RNE×NE\mat{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}}N∈RNE​×NE​ of standard normals, adding 2Δt/cNΘ~\sqrt{2 \Delta t / c} \mat{N} \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}2Δt/c​NΘ~ gives each member the covariance 2ΔtΣ^θ2 \Delta t \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta2ΔtΣ^θ​, and no Dθ×DθD_\theta \times D_\thetaDθ​×Dθ​ Cholesky factor is formed.

  4. The prior, taken implicitly as θ←θ−(I+ΔtΣ^θΣθ−1)−1ΔtΣ^θΣθ−1(θ−μθ)\gvect{\theta} \leftarrow \gvect{\theta} - (\mat{I} + \Delta t \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1})^{-1} \Delta t \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1} (\gvect{\theta} - \gvect{\mu}_\theta)θ←θ−(I+ΔtΣ^θ​Σθ−1​)−1ΔtΣ^θ​Σθ−1​(θ−μθ​). A push-through identity reduces the solve to NE×NEN_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}NE​×NE​, and a prior much tighter than the ensemble then cannot destabilise the step.

The step sets the bias¶

Take a scalar linear model with a flat prior, large NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ and precision γ=H⊤Σε−1H\gamma = \mat{H}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \mat{H}γ=H⊤Σε−1​H. Over one step the data term divides an anomaly by 1+ΔtΣ^θγ1 + \Delta t \hat{\Sigma}_\theta \gamma1+ΔtΣ^θ​γ, and the noise adds 2ΔtΣ^θ2 \Delta t \hat{\Sigma}_\theta2ΔtΣ^θ​ to the variance, so a stationary variance solves

Σ^θ=Σ^θ(1+ΔtΣ^θγ)2+2ΔtΣ^θ.\hat{\Sigma}_\theta = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}_\theta}{(1 + \Delta t \hat{\Sigma}_\theta \gamma)^2} + 2 \Delta t \hat{\Sigma}_\theta.Σ^θ​=(1+ΔtΣ^θ​γ)2Σ^θ​​+2ΔtΣ^θ​.
(9.18)

Dividing by Σ^θ\hat{\Sigma}_\thetaΣ^θ​ and solving gives

Σ^θγ=(1−2Δt)−1/2−1Δt≈1+32Δt,\hat{\Sigma}_\theta \gamma = \frac{(1 - 2 \Delta t)^{-1/2} - 1}{\Delta t} \approx 1 + \frac{3}{2} \Delta t,Σ^θ​γ=Δt(1−2Δt)−1/2−1​≈1+23​Δt,
(9.19)

and no stationary solution for Δt≥1/2\Delta t \ge 1 / 2Δt≥1/2, where the variance grows at every step. Program 9.15 confirms both. So EKS samples a biased posterior, by an amount the step controls, and that is the job of its scheduler.

Schedulers¶

Every process takes its Δt(i)\Delta t^{(i)}Δt(i) from an AbstractScheduler, which reads the current ProcessState and returns a scalar.

FixedScheduler(dt) returns a constant, which you tune. With dt=1.0 one step of EKI or UKI is the full Kalman update, and the Layer 2 run stops there.

DataMisfitController is the rule of Iglesias & Yang (2021), with no tuning parameter. With the cost of each member, J(e)=12∥y−h(e)∥Σε−12\mathcal{J}^{(e)} = \frac{1}{2} \Vert \vect{y} - \vect{h}^{(e)} \Vert^2_{\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1}}J(e)=21​∥y−h(e)∥Σε−1​2​, and its ensemble mean Jˉ\bar{\mathcal{J}}Jˉ​ and variance σJ2\sigma_\mathcal{J}^2σJ2​,

Δt(i)=min⁡(max⁡(Dy2Jˉ,Dy2σJ2),1−τ(i)).\Delta t^{(i)} = \min\left(\max\left(\frac{D_y}{2 \bar{\mathcal{J}}}, \sqrt{\frac{D_y}{2 \sigma_\mathcal{J}^2}}\right), 1 - \tau^{(i)}\right).Δt(i)=min(max(2Jˉ​Dy​​,2σJ2​Dy​​​),1−τ(i)).
(9.20)

Both candidates come from 2J2 \mathcal{J}2J being χ2\chi^2χ2 with DyD_yDy​ degrees of freedom under the correct model, which has mean DyD_yDy​ and variance 2Dy2 D_y2Dy​. The steps are small while the members are far from the data, they grow as the misfit falls, and the clamp lands τ\tauτ exactly on 1. After that the rule returns Δt=0\Delta t = 0Δt=0, and filterax floors the step at 10-30, so that further calls change nothing and give no NaN. The computation is gaussx.discrepancy_step_size, which applies Σε−1\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1}Σε−1​ through a structured solve.

EKSStableScheduler bounds the step by the ensemble covariance and by the stiffness of the posterior:

Δt(i)=min⁡(Δtmax,a∥Σ^θ∥F,b∥S∥F),S=1c(H~Σε−1H~⊤+Θ~Σθ−1Θ~⊤),\Delta t^{(i)} = \min\left(\Delta t_\text{max}, \frac{a}{\Vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta \Vert_F}, \frac{b}{\Vert \mat{S} \Vert_F}\right), \qquad \mat{S} = \frac{1}{c} \left(\tilde{\mat{H}} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top + \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}} \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1} \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^\top\right),Δt(i)=min(Δtmax​,∥Σ^θ​∥F​a​,∥S∥F​b​),S=c1​(H~Σε−1​H~⊤+Θ~Σθ−1​Θ~⊤),
(9.21)

with S∈RNE×NE\mat{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}}S∈RNE​×NE​, where Δtmax\Delta t_\text{max}Δtmax​, aaa and bbb are the arguments max_dt, target and target_stiffness. The prior term in S\mat{S}S appears only when the state carries a prior. For a linear hhh, S\mat{S}S has the nonzero spectrum of Σ^θ(Λh+Σθ−1)\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta (\gmat{\Lambda}_h + \gmat{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1})Σ^θ​(Λh​+Σθ−1​), so at the exact posterior ∥S∥F=Dθ\Vert \mat{S} \Vert_F = \sqrt{D_\theta}∥S∥F​=Dθ​​ whatever the scale of the problem. The step then settles at about b/Dθb / \sqrt{D_\theta}b/Dθ​​, and the default b=0.1b = 0.1b=0.1 aims through (9.19) for an excess variance of about 10% on a low-dimensional, data-dominated problem.

Implementation in filterax¶

The processes come at three levels, built on one set of update rules.

LayerOffersWho runs hhh
filterax.processesEKI, ETKI, GNKI, TEKI, SparseInversion, EKS_Process and UKI, each with init and updateyou, so you control batching, checkpoints and dispatch
filteraxEKI, TEKI, EKS and UKI, each with runthe run loop, through vmap
filterax.optaxeki, eks and uki, as optax.GradientTransformationthe transformation, ignoring grads

The Layer 2 EKI and UKI default to DataMisfitController, stop at τ≥1\tau \ge 1τ≥1, and allow 50 iterations. TEKI and EKS always run their full budget, 200 and 500 iterations by default, because neither has a reason to stop at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1. Passing a ProcessConfig overrides the scheduler and the budget together. ETKI, GNKI and SparseInversion have no Layer 2 wrapper.

The example is the linear problem used through this chapter, with Dθ=2D_\theta = 2Dθ​=2, Dy=3D_y = 3Dy​=3 and 200 members drawn from a wide prior.

It prints 4 True, [0.0169 0.0964 0.4656 1. ] and [ 1.1542 -1.1028] for EKI, then 4 [ 1.2307 -1.164 ] for UKI. The controller takes four steps, each several times the last, and lands on τ=1\tau = 1τ=1. The two means differ because of (9.6), and only UKI’s is the Kalman mean.

Layer 1 leaves the loop to you, and each update takes the forward evaluations. It compiles, where the Layer 2 EKI.run calls float on τ\tauτ and so raises a ConcretizationTypeError under jax.jit. Program 9.2 runs a fixed number of steps inside one jax.lax.scan, and later blocks reuse the helper. The optax form keeps the ensemble in its state and returns the change in the mean as the update. It ignores the gradient argument, so it composes with other optax transformations.

It prints 1.0 True, then 0.0, then 1.0 [ 1.1523 -1.0971]. Layer 1 reproduces Layer 2, and another update at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1 moves nothing. The optax result differs a little because transform.init draws its own ensemble around params.

Algorithm¶

Program 9.3 writes out one step of (9.3) in dense form, and compares it with the Layer 1 update at Δt=0.25\Delta t = 0.25Δt=0.25.

It prints True.

Agreement with the Kalman update¶

With a linear hhh the reference is a dense Kalman update of the initial mean and sample covariance, which Program 9.4 computes in numpy along with the limit (9.6). The table splits the budget ∑iΔt(i)=1\sum_i \Delta t^{(i)} = 1∑i​Δt(i)=1 into NiterN_\text{iter}Niter​ equal steps.

It prints:

The variance columns are tr(Σ^θ)\op{tr}(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta)tr(Σ^θ​) over the Kalman value. ETKI and UKI are exact for every split, as (9.8) says. EKI has the Kalman mean only at one step, and its variance there is 1.5% of the Kalman variance. With many small steps the variance tends to about a half, the value of (9.5) when the data dominate, and the mean error grows instead. The last line prints limit 2.7e-04 1.5e-04, the gap between 256 EKI steps and the closed-form limit, in the mean and in the covariance. UKI is given a ProcessConfig, because a schedule that needs more steps than the budget of 50 stops early with converged false.

EKS against the posterior¶

Program 9.9 runs the sampler on the same posterior with its default scheduler, and averages over the second half of the run. A long run under a scan takes seconds, where the Layer 2 run is a Python loop.

It prints [ 1.2124 -1.1616] [0.0576 0.0596], then 0.0170, then 0.959 34.17, then 0.0707 0.0707 0.0707. The mean is within 0.017 of the exact posterior, and the total variance is 0.96 of the exact one, over a run reaching τ≈34\tau \approx 34τ≈34. (9.19) predicts an excess of about 10% for a flat prior and a large ensemble. This run has neither, so it does not test that number, and Program 9.15 does. The last line is the scheduler at the exact posterior for noise variances of 0.1 and 10-4, next to b/Dθb / \sqrt{D_\theta}b/Dθ​​. The step does not depend on the scale of the problem, as (9.21) claims.

A nonlinear problem against a grid¶

With Dθ=2D_\theta = 2Dθ​=2 the posterior of a nonlinear model can be computed on a grid, which gives a reference for all of them at once. The model is

h(θ)=[θ0+0.3θ12θ1+0.3θ02θ0θ1],h(\gvect{\theta}) = \begin{bmatrix} \theta_0 + 0.3 \theta_1^2 \\ \theta_1 + 0.3 \theta_0^2 \\ \theta_0 \theta_1 \end{bmatrix},h(θ)=⎣⎡​θ0​+0.3θ12​θ1​+0.3θ02​θ0​θ1​​⎦⎤​,
(9.22)

with a standard normal prior and a noise variance of 0.1.

It prints the grid posterior, [ 0.8699 -0.5688] [0.0602 0.0596], and then:

The exactness of ETKI and UKI is gone, and what remains is a statistical linearisation. Here UKI does much the best per evaluation, and EKS has the smallest error in the mean for the largest bill. This nonlinearity is mild, and a stronger one may rank them differently.

Numerics: float32, sigma points and gradients¶

ETKI’s transform and UKI’s standard form behave differently when the observations are strong. UKI subtracts two nearly equal covariances in (9.10), while ETKI works through the eigenvalues of Λw\gmat{\Lambda}_wΛw​ (chapter 6). Program 9.11 measures both against a float64 reference in information form, since the dense update of Program 9.4 itself loses digits to the same subtraction.

It prints:

σ2\sigma^2σ2ETKI meanETKI covarianceUKI meanUKI covariance
10-19e-081e-065e-086e-07
10-31e-071e-062e-078e-06
10-61e-073e-052e-042e-02
10-84e-072e-041e-017e+02

With a prior variance of about 4, ordinary noise is fine in either form. As the noise falls UKI loses its covariance first, and at σ2=10−8\sigma^2 = 10^{-8}σ2=10−8 that covariance is meaningless while ETKI still has three digits. The pattern fits the subtraction, but that reading is an interpretation and not a separate test. In float64 this is not a concern at these sizes, and for strong observations in float32 ETKI is the safer form.

The sigma-point weights matter more than the update does. At α=1\alpha = 1α=1 the centre mean weight is zero, while at α=10−3\alpha = 10^{-3}α=10−3 it is about -106, and the moments come out of a cancellation between weights of that size. gaussx warns about that in float32, and the UKI docstring’s suggestion of a small α\alphaα for a very nonlinear hhh runs against that warning.

It prints [ 0.8628 -0.6138] in both precisions at α=1\alpha = 1α=1, and at α=10−3\alpha = 10^{-3}α=10−3 it prints [ 0.8697 -0.6216] in float64 and [ 0.8589 -0.6157] in float32. So α=1\alpha = 1α=1 loses nothing to float32, and α=10−3\alpha = 10^{-3}α=10−3 is wrong in the third digit. The two values of α\alphaα also differ from each other in float64, since they are different quadratures of a nonlinear hhh.

The steps themselves are differentiable, including the adaptive rule, because the min and max in (9.20) only choose between smooth branches. So a Layer 1 loop can sit inside a gradient, which Program 9.13 checks against a central difference for EKI under the adaptive rule.

It prints -0.565514 -0.565514.

When it breaks¶

Past the stopping time, EKI fits the noise. On an ill-conditioned problem the least-squares fit is far from the truth. An unregularised iteration heads for that fit once it has used up the useful part of the data. This is why τ=1\tau = 1τ=1 is a stopping rule and not a formality. Program 9.14 uses Dθ=Dy=8D_\theta = D_y = 8Dθ​=Dy​=8, with singular values from 1 down to about 3×10−43 \times 10^{-4}3×10−4 and a noise standard deviation of 0.01.

It prints:

Iterationsτ\tauτEKI errorTEKI error
1012.632.36
100103.762.33
10001007.802.32
10000100013.052.31

and then 20.30 2.31, the errors of the least-squares fit and of the MAP. EKI at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1 has an error about that of the MAP, and it heads for the fit if allowed. The Layer 2 EKI stops at τ=1\tau = 1τ=1 and so never sees this, while TEKI holds still because its cost has a minimum to hold on to.

A large EKS step has no stationary law. Program 9.15 runs a scalar model with γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 and 200 members and compares the variance with (9.19), then crosses the limit at Δt=1/2\Delta t = 1 / 2Δt=1/2.

It prints 0.1 1.15 1.180, 0.4 3.13 3.090 and 0.6 1.69e+76 nan, with the measured variance before the formula’s. Below the limit the two agree within the sampling and the finite-ensemble pull, and a step of 0.4 triples the variance with no warning. Above the limit nothing is stationary and the run diverges, which EKSStableScheduler exists to prevent.

GNKI’s jitter breaks a long run. δ\deltaδ in (9.11) is absolute. Once Σ^θ\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\thetaΣ^θ​ falls below δ\deltaδ, the estimate J^h\hat{\mat{J}}_hJ^h​ goes to zero, then G\mat{G}G goes to zero, and (9.12) pulls every member back to the prior mean. This is a bug rather than a limit of the method. At Δt=1\Delta t = 1Δt=1 the second step already jumps to the prior mean, as Program 9.16 shows. Stop after the step that reaches τ=1\tau = 1τ=1, and do not run GNKI with a fixed step past that.

It prints [ 1.2294 -1.1584] after one step at Δt=1\Delta t = 1Δt=1, and [ 0. -0.] after two. At Δt=0.5\Delta t = 0.5Δt=0.5 it prints [ 1.2247 -1.1541] after 8 steps, and [0.4234 0.0199] after 16. The exact posterior mean is [ 1.2294 -1.1584], so more iterations are moving away from the answer.

SparseInversion shrinks everything if it runs on. The threshold in (9.16) does not fade with the spread. Once the data term has stopped moving the members, the active parameters keep losing ϱΔt\varrho \Delta tϱΔt a step. Program 9.17 has two active parameters out of five.

It prints 5 [ 1.96 0. 0. -1.454 0. ], 100 [ 1.252 0. 0. -0.676 0. ] and 500 [0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]. At τ=1\tau = 1τ=1, after 5 steps, the support is right and the active values are close. By 500 steps every parameter is zero, and an ensemble of zeros cannot move again, because it has no anomalies.

Three other limits are worth knowing:

  • A small ensemble confines EKI, ETKI and TEKI to its span, so what the initial anomalies cannot express stays unreachable.

  • A strongly nonlinear hhh leaves ETKI and UKI as statistical linearisations, and their exactness above is a statement about linear models only.

  • EKS has a bias from its step, and its members are correlated in time, so its average needs a burn-in and a long run.
